content:
Earlier this year, I swapped my battery-powered mower for a robotic mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. You can manually drive it around the perimeter of your yard to create a virtual map. Once set up, it automatically starts mowing according to a preset schedule.

I have also previously tried another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different approach to navigation, and after several weeks of testing, I think it may be a simpler option for many users.

Automatic camera mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 that I reviewed earlier this year lies in how each machine understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses RTK base station positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower around the perimeter with my iPhone to build the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the company calls TerraVision 2.0. Equipped with three cameras, the mower is able to automatically map out the lawn and navigate without the need to install boundary wires or additional RTK antennas.

The automatic initial mapping process does indeed take longer. However, for people who are not particularly tech-savvy, this approach may be easier to get started with.

To test this idea, I asked my mum, who lives in another state, to set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own, without any help from me. She replied that everything worked smoothly. That said, I do find it harder to judge whether she would have had the patience to first manually drive the mower around the entire perimeter and then manually mark out the areas to avoid.

During the automatic mapping process, a small issue came up in my front yard. There is no fence or any other physical separation between my lawn and my neighbour's, so the TerraMow initially incorporated a portion of the neighbour's lawn into my map.

I later resolved this by setting that area as a no-go zone in the app. That said, if your lawn does not have clear visual boundaries, you need to pay close attention during the initial mapping period.

Remote camera monitoring via the app

The cameras on the TerraMow also make one of my favourite features possible. The iPhone app can show a live view of what the mower sees while it is working.

During testing, I used the iPhone Mirroring feature on my Mac to keep this view open in a large window. I could work indoors while watching, from the mower's perspective, as it moved around the back garden.

This feature is not essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more engaging and can also help explain why it slows down or avoids certain things. The Anthbot M9 has no equivalent camera view feature.

The two iPhone apps have a lot in common. Both let you schedule working times, adjust mowing behaviour, divide zones, mark no-go areas, and control the mower remotely.

Speaking of that last feature, the TerraMow has a particularly thoughtful design detail. In addition to the conventional left-right virtual controls, its app also offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and steer with your thumb.

Manually controlling the mower with an iPhone is not the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically according to a preset schedule without any intervention. However, using the TerraMow's joystick to touch up missed spots is genuinely a pleasure.

Sometimes I almost feel as if I am controlling the robot with telekinesis (it really does feel that good). I can hold the iPhone by my side, give a gentle 'go' with my thumb, and the mower will move according to my instructions.

Every robotic mower app should take note of this kind of control design.

More aggressive mowing performance

The TerraMow V1000 also mowed more aggressively than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was noticeably louder while working.

I would not say the TerraMow is loud. But the difference between the two is quite obvious. The Anthbot can run extremely quietly, almost making you forget it is still there, even when it is mowing at night with its headlight on.

Because the TerraMow relies on camera-based navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. As a result, scheduling daytime runs becomes even more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and well-built. It is also larger than the Anthbot M9. The TerraMow comes with a cover that can shield the charging dock, whereas the Anthbot's cover has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has been consistently stable and reliable. I have relied on it for several weeks in a row and have not mowed the lawn myself since.

When adaptive mapping is a little too 'clever'

The visual intelligence that makes the TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continuously adjusts the map based on what it sees. Each time a run is finished, saving these changes takes a little time, during which you temporarily cannot do anything in the app.

After a few days of rain, I ran into an interesting quirk. Puddles had formed in parts of the yard, and the TerraMow cleverly avoided those areas during its next run.

The grass inside the skipped circular patches then grew taller. After a while, the mower seemed to treat that tuft of tall grass as something to keep avoiding, so even after the ground had dried out, that tuft was still being ignored.

I used the app's remote control feature to manually mow that tuft of tall grass, and the problem was resolved. Once the grass returned to normal, automatic mowing resumed working normally in that spot as well.

Regular edging can also help the TerraMow operate closer to the boundaries. If you do not trim, tall grass near the edges may be mistaken for obstacles rather than mowing areas.

The Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive and relies more heavily on the boundaries and obstacles that I set up myself. This method requires more upfront work, but it avoids situations where the map 'changes its mind' and refuses to mow a certain patch of grass.

9to5Mac perspective

Having used both systems, for most people I lean toward the TerraMow's camera-based approach.

For me, laying down boundary wires is completely off the table, and installing an RTK base station means one more piece of hardware to place, power, and maintain. The TerraMow needs neither.

Its visual navigation is not perfect. The initial mapping takes longer, unclear boundaries need manual correction, and the adaptive behaviour has mistakenly treated overly tall grass as a permanent obstacle.

These issues are still manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, engaging live camera footage, and the best manual controls I have seen in any robotic mower app.

I genuinely enjoy yard maintenance, but mowing is the most repetitive part of it. Handing that part over to a robot means I can spend more time on landscaping, edging, and detail work, while still keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 delivers on this, so I can recommend it, especially for anyone who wants a robotic mower but does not want to lay down boundary wires, install an RTK antenna, or manually walk an iPhone around the entire yard.

Amazon is currently selling the TerraMow V1000 with a promotional code. After entering the $200 off code on the site, the price drops to $999. You can also purchase it through TerraMow's official website.
